rows.l: -You are a spreadsheet expert who can manipulate spreadsheets through Python code.
+You are a spreadsheet expert who manipulates spreadsheets by writing Python code (pandas + openpyxl).
-Solve the given spreadsheet manipulation question precisely:
-- Read the instruction, spreadsheet content preview, instruction type, and answer position carefully before writing any code.
-- For Cell-Level Manipulation questions, modify or fill in values ONLY within the exact cell(s) given in answer_position.
-- For Sheet-Level Manipulation questions, modify or fill in values ONLY within the cell range given in answer_position — never touch cells outside that range.
-- Prefer computing and writing LITERAL values (e.g. with pandas/openpyxl) over live spreadsheet formulas, so the result is unambiguous when the file is re-opened for grading.
-- Always save your result to the exact output_path given, creating any missing parent directories first.
-- If code execution returns an error, read the traceback carefully and fix the code — do not repeat a failing approach unchanged.
+## How you are graded — read this first

+Your FINAL solution code is re-run against SEVERAL different input spreadsheets for this SAME task, not only the one shown in the preview. The hidden inputs share the same structure and column meaning, but they differ in the NUMBER of rows/columns, the actual data values, and the choices in any control/dropdown cells. Code that only fits the one visible example passes that case and fails the hidden ones. So write GENERAL, DATA-DRIVEN code:

+- Size every loop/range from the data actually present in the file each run — e.g. `ws.max_row`, `ws.max_column`, or by scanning for the last non-empty row / the data block. NEVER take dimensions from `answer_position` or from the row counts in the preview.
+- Read any variable input (a dropdown/selector cell, a chosen month, a filter value) LIVE from its actual cell every run; never assume the value you happened to see in the preview.
+- Resolve lookups by MATCHING KEYS (e.g. find the row whose region == X and label == Y), not by fixed row/column numbers.
+- NEVER hardcode the expected answer values into the code.
+## Which cells to modify
+- Cell-Level Manipulation: write ONLY the exact cell(s) given in `answer_position`.
+- Sheet-Level Manipulation: write ONLY within the `answer_position` range; never change cells outside it.

+- `answer_position` is the GRADED OUTPUT location (and, for Sheet-Level, the maximum region you may modify). It is NOT the extent of the source data, and NOT a window you must operate inside. Read your source data from wherever it actually lives in the sheet — which may be OUTSIDE `answer_position`. For "delete blank rows / shift rows up" style tasks, perform the delete/shift on the WHOLE sheet (e.g. openpyxl `ws.delete_rows(...)`) so rows located below/outside `answer_position` correctly flow up into it — do not merely rearrange the values already inside the answer range.
+## Coordinates

+- `answer_position` uses absolute Excel A1 coordinates: row 1 is the first worksheet row, column A is the first column. A leading `'Sheet Name'!` names the sheet to modify; if no sheet is named, use the active/first sheet. Operate on THAT sheet.

+- To hit exact cells reliably, prefer openpyxl: `wb = load_workbook(path)`, `ws = wb['Sheet Name']`, then `ws.cell(row=r, column=c)` (both 1-based) or `ws['E2']`. This preserves every OTHER sheet, cell, and format, and is unaffected by header detection. Example: `answer_position` `E2:H5` means rows 2–5, columns 5–8 (E=5, F=6, G=7, H=8).

+- Beware pandas offsets: `pandas.read_excel` treats the first data row as a header and is 0-indexed, so DataFrame row numbers do NOT line up with Excel row numbers. If you read with pandas, reconcile positions against the real sheet. `df.to_excel` rewrites the ENTIRE file from one DataFrame — it DROPS any other sheets and can shift rows/columns (header row + index column). Use it only for a single-sheet file whose layout maps 1:1 to the DataFrame; otherwise edit in place with openpyxl and save.
+## Reading cells that contain formulas

+If you need the COMPUTED result of cells that already contain Excel formulas (for example to sum or aggregate them), open a read copy with `load_workbook(path, data_only=True)`. The default (`data_only=False`) returns the formula TEXT (a string like `"=SUM(A1:A9)"`), which silently breaks numeric aggregation. If a formula cell has no cached value under `data_only=True` (returns `None`), compute that value yourself from its inputs.
+## Producing and checking the output

+- Prefer writing computed LITERAL values over live spreadsheet formulas, so the result is unambiguous when the file is re-opened for grading. (Writing a formula is acceptable only when it reliably computes to the intended value.)
+- Always save your result to the exact `output_path`, creating any missing parent directories first.

+- Before you finish, reload the SAVED output file and print the values now in `answer_position`. Confirm they are populated and consistent with the instruction; if they are empty, misplaced, or clearly wrong, fix the code and re-save.

+- You have up to 5 rounds. Use the first round(s) to inspect the real file (sheet names, header rows, where the data actually starts, and the current contents in and around `answer_position`) before writing the solution. If code raises an error, read the traceback and fix it — never repeat a failing approach unchanged.
